newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh sees political stability, higher growth.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh sees political stability, higher growth.

text.p: Bangladesh's economy, which has marked time in the past quarter of a century, is expected to break out of its rut with the help of relative political stability and economic reforms, economists said.
The country, which continues to grapple with rampant poverty, will celebrate the silver jubilee of its independence from Pakistan on Monday.
Nearly half of Bangladesh's 120 million population remains below the internationally designated poverty line.
A series of military coups, poor economic management and political unrest have had hurt the country's growth despite huge inflows of foreign assistance over the decades.

Economists and government officials, however, see better days ahead, saying the country's economy is set to expand more than five percent this year and the next, fired by signs of political stability and the government's vow to pursue reforms.

"I think the economy will grow at least 5.5 percent this year. This will be crossing the five percent barrier for the first time in many, many years," Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told Reuters in an weekend interview.
"Inshallah (God willing), the growth rate will exceed 6.0 percent next year," he said.
The country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) has remained stagnant at around four percent since 1971, when Bangladesh won independence following a nine-month war.
The minister said there had been a lack of significant reforms in government administration and the judiciary.
"Without administrative reforms, (a) development programme will not succeed. Judicial reforms are essential in order to give confidence to investors," he said.
"We have decided to change the basic strategy. We will put the private sector in the driver's seat," he said.

"We have to bring in foreign investment and move in a resolute way. We have decided to amend the laws for loan courts and make it easier for settlement of financial disputes. The government has already prepared bankruptcy laws," he added.
Kibria was made finance minister after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's Awami League swept to power in June this year.
Bangladesh has since seen unprecedented political stability.
"The country is passing through an era of political peace. People are quite confident about the government's policies towards development and progress," one analyst said.

Qazi Kholiquzzaman, Chairman of the Bangladesh Unnayan Parishad (development council) think-tank, told Reuters: "Despite substantial reforms carried out since (the) late 1980s, the economic growth rates averaged about four percent in the 1990s, no better than in (the) 1980s or the 1970s."

He said the reform programmes pursued by the previous government failed to address problems in the agriculture sector "which is most important not only in terms of (the) population dependence on it but also in terms of generation of purchasing power to support goods and services produced in other sectors."
Seventy percent of the country's population are dependent on agriculture.
"The government should undertake appropriate reform programmes which must include both macro-economic aspects as well as peoples' priorities at (the) micro level," Kholiquzzaman said.

Pierre Landell-Mills, World Bank mission chief in Dhaka, said Bangladesh performed better than many of the World Bank's loan receiving countries despite its stagnant growth rates in the past. "More people are better off now," he said.
"The economy is moving towards (the) right direction. Recent pick up in imports also suggests that investment will be picking up," he told Reuters.
